Iranian media cited spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying that Iran was working with Oman on "mechanisms for monitoring security, protecting the environment and combating crime at sea." Fees would be for maritime services provided to ships, he explained. The dispute over transit rights in the strait, through which some 20% of the world's oil passed before the war and which is a key route for gas and fertilizer, is regarded as a key reason behind the continuation of the war against Iran. What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Before the United States and Israel launched the conflict against Iran at the end of February, shipping through the waterway did no incur tolls nor fees for transit. The Strait of Hormuz measures only around 39 kilometers (24 miles) at its narrowest point. Since Iran and Oman each claim the maximum 12 nautical miles allowed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) as their territorial waters, there are no international waters in the narrowest part of the roughly 21-nautical-mile-wide strait. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees a right of transit passage and prohibits a blockade of commercial vessels. Iran, however, does not accept this legal position. https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/mi.text: A man destroyed a petrol station's chip-and-pin machine after a cashier allegedly made a 'go back to Romania' jibe. Adrian-Costinel Rotaru said he'd been using Texaco Garage in Smethwick for around 16 years prior to the incident on November 15, 2025. The 39-year-old had gone to fill up at around 9.30am, but became 'quite unhappy' when he was asked to make a payment first. READ MORE: Man, 21, 'drowned after vanishing from Twitch event during trip' Rotaru claimed when he questioned why other customers hadn't been asked to do the same, he was told 'If you don't like it, go back to Romania'. Dudley Magistrates' Court heard Rotaru had picked up the chip and pin machine and ‘threw it on the floor’. After breaking the machine, which was valued at around £200, Rotaru left the petrol station and drove away. Rotaru, of Francis Road, Ladywood, pleaded guilty to criminal damage during the hearing on July 30. The court was told Rotaru was of 'previous good character'. His legal representative said: “He has visited this petrol station for 16 years. "It was early morning, and for some reason, he was asked to pay first, although numerous people were filling up without having to pay first." The court was told Rotaru had said 'You’re not asking anyone else, why are you asking me to pay first?’ He was allegedly told ‘If you don’t like it, go back to Romania’ in response. A magistrate told Rotaru: “We are taking into account your previous good character. “We have had a chance to listen to how it all occurred and we are going to go with a compensation order. “It was a silly moment, the best thing is to draw a line under it and carry on.” Rotaru was ordered to pay £200 compensation and £85 court costs.

https://www.techtimes.com/articles/32660.text: A collective action worth £2 billion filed by developers (approximately $2.71 billion USD) landed at London's Competition Appeal Tribunal on September 3, 2026, accusing Apple of engineering the consent prompts inside its App Tracking Transparency framework to systematically steer iPhone users away from third-party tracking — while leaving Apple's own advertising operations free from the same friction. The claim landed three weeks after Germany became the first competition authority in the world to extract Apple ATT binding commitments from Germany to redesign exactly those prompts, handing UK developers a body of evidence they intend to build their damages case on.The vehicle bringing the claim is ATT Collective Action Limited, directed by Ann Pope — who spent a decade as a senior CMA antitrust director at the UK's own Competition and Markets Authority before leaving in 2024. Law firm Hausfeld, which in October 2025 secured a £1.5 billion App Store verdict — the first successful collective action under the UK's competition class-action regime — is acting for the claimants here as well.Apple's Dual-Consent Architecture: The Technical Claim at the Center of the CaseApp Tracking Transparency, introduced by Apple with iOS 14.5 in April 2021, requires third-party apps that wish to track a user's activity across other companies' apps and websites to display an Apple-designed pop-up consent prompt. If the user declines, the app is denied access to the device's Identifier for Advertisers — the IDFA — which is the only technically viable mechanism through which an app can track behavior across different companies' platforms.What the UK claim centers on is a structural asymmetry in how Apple applied this framework. Third-party apps were required to obtain consent twice: first under data protection law (GDPR-equivalent consent for collecting user data), and then again through Apple's additional ATT prompt. Apple's own services — including its App Store search advertising and its "Personalized Ads" system — were not subject to this double-consent requirement, because Apple's own advertising does not use the IDFA and does not combine data across third-party companies.The claimants argue that this architecture was not a neutral privacy design but a tilted competitive mechanism. Apple's own prompt, shown to users about its own data-collection practices, used neutral language. Third-party apps were required to use Apple-predesigned language that included a warning hand symbol and the word "tracking" — a term that Germany's Federal Cartel Office found specifically discouraging to users and gave Apple's own consent mechanism a material competitive advantage.Germany's August 2026 Ruling: How the Bundeskartellamt's Finding Became a Roadmap for the UK ClaimThe timing of the UK filing — exactly three weeks after Germany announced binding commitments from Apple — is not coincidental. On August 17, 2026, Germany's Federal Cartel Office formally declared legally binding a set of Apple ATT commitments under which Apple agreed to rebuild the consent prompt shown by third-party apps: removing the warning hand symbol, removing the word "tracking," allowing publishers to add up to 4,000 characters explaining why personalized advertising funds their apps, and giving developers three defined ways to combine the ATT prompt with GDPR consent requests into a single pop-up rather than the cumbersome double-ask that had been required.The underlying decision carries the date of August 13, 2026, and the case reference B7-54/25. Apple has four months from service to implement the changes across Germany and, per Apple's own statement, in almost all other EU countries as well. An independent trustee will monitor compliance for seven years.Andreas Mundt, President of the Bundeskartellamt, set out the principle underlying the German decision: Apple is permitted to provide users with privacy protections exceeding the legal minimum, but any additional rules Apple sets for data use within its ecosystem must not treat Apple's own offerings better than those of its competitors — an obligation that flows from Germany's special abuse provision for large digital companies.Apple did not concede infringement in Germany. The company said it believed the existing ATT prompt was clear and effective and that its position was shared by German data protection authorities — but agreed to change the wording and design anyway. The proceeding ended without a fine.For the UK developers' claim, however, the German outcome is potentially significant as a matter of evidence. The Bundeskartellamt's formal finding — that the IDFA is the only mechanism for cross-company data exchange on iOS, and that Apple's prompt wording was not competitively neutral — gives claimants in London a template for what they will argue a UK court should also conclude. The UK claim, unlike Germany's proceeding, seeks damages for losses already suffered rather than forward-looking behavioral changes.What Privacy Cost the Industry: The £2 Billion Claim in ContextAnn Pope, speaking on behalf of ATT Collective Action Limited on Thursday, described the stakes in a statement from the ATT claimants: "The ATT policy was implemented without the transparency and objectivity you would expect from a company in Apple's position, and it resulted in very significant harm to businesses that depend on Apple as a gatekeeper."She also addressed the privacy framing head-on: "Privacy is an important protection for consumers, but it should be applied fairly and in a way that ensures businesses of all sizes can compete on a level playing field. It cannot become a reason for digital platforms to play by one set of rules while forcing app developers to play by another."The industry-level damage from ATT is well-documented in the advertising economics literature. A November 2021 analysis by advertising technology company Lotame, first reported by the Financial Times, estimated that Snapchat, Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube collectively lost approximately $9.85 billion in advertising revenue in the second half of 2021 alone — a combined 12% revenue reduction across those four platforms in the quarters immediately following ATT's launch. Facebook lost the most in absolute dollar terms; Snap suffered the worst percentage hit because its entire advertising business was smartphone-dependent.Simultaneously, Apple's own App Store Search Ads business — which is not subject to the ATT prompt requirement — roughly tripled its share of iPhone advertising in the six months after ATT launched, as advertisers redirected budgets away from platforms that had lost IDFA-based targeting capability and toward Apple's own ad product, which faces none of that friction.The UK claim specifically covers app developers based in Britain. The size of that class has not been publicly stated; Hausfeld's filings describe it as encompassing "thousands" of UK-based businesses. Unlike a US class action that requires individual members to opt in, the UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal collective proceedings regime operates as opt-out: every eligible UK-domiciled app developer is automatically included in the claim unless they affirmatively step out. That mechanism — introduced by the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and enabled at the CAT from October of that year — is the same legal architecture that made the £1.5 billion ($2.03 billion) Kent v Apple consumer verdict possible last October.Apple's Three UK Lawsuits, and the Regulatory Map Across EuropeThe ATT filing is now the third major collective action Apple faces at the Competition Appeal Tribunal simultaneously. The consumer-side App Store claim — the landmark case brought by Dr. Rachael Kent on behalf of approximately 36 million UK iPhone and iPad users, alleging the 30% commission on purchases was excessive and unlawful — produced a judgment against Apple in October 2025 for up to £1.5 billion ($2.03 billion); Apple has escalated its appeal to the Court of Appeal after the CAT declined to grant an internal appeal. A separate developer-side claim over App Store commission fees brought by Sean Ennis, professor at the University of East Anglia, is also ongoing at the tribunal. The Which? iCloud action at CAT is not yet scheduled for trial.Across Europe, the ATT framework has generated a consistent pattern of regulatory action over four years, each jurisdiction taking a slightly different approach:France imposed a €150 million fine over ATT (approximately $174 million USD) in March 2025 after its competition authority, the Autorité de la concurrence, found ATT was not applied consistently but stopped short of ordering a prompt redesign. Italy imposed a €98.6 million ATT abuse fine (approximately $114 million USD) in December 2025 and additionally required Apple to immediately cease its anti-competitive conduct — the most operationally demanding of the three regulatory outcomes. Germany took the most structurally significant step of all, obtaining the binding redesign commitments described above. Regulators in Poland and Romania have also examined the framework; no decisions from those jurisdictions have been published.The UK's CMA has not formally fined Apple over ATT as of this writing. That gap leaves open the possibility of a parallel domestic regulatory investigation proceeding alongside the private damages claim now before the tribunal.The competitive backdrop shifted in August as well: Google's £260 million Play Store settlement — reached last month between Alphabet and UK Android app developers who alleged Google had exploited its Play Store dominance to overcharge them on commissions — signals that the CAT's platform accountability regime is generating real financial consequences across the market, not just for Apple.Did Apple Play by Different Rules? What the Claim AllegesThe claimants in ATT Collective Action Limited v Apple allege that the framework's design served two simultaneous goals: presenting a privacy credential for Apple's brand, and neutralizing the advertising economics of competitors by making consent burdensome to obtain for their apps while leaving Apple's own advertising business operating on an easier consent track.Apple's consistent position is that the exemption is structurally justified. Its own advertising products — App Store search ads, placement in the Maps application, advertising in Apple News — do not use the IDFA. They are based on data Apple already holds about its users' App Store behavior and do not combine information from third-party sources. Therefore, Apple argues, the cross-company tracking framework that ATT governs simply does not apply to its own ad operations. Third-party apps not engaged in cross-company tracking are equally exempt from showing the ATT prompt, the company says. Apple dismissed the UK claim as meritless in its initial response.Whether that structural argument survives scrutiny at the certification stage — and eventually at trial — will depend in part on how the CAT interprets the Bundeskartellamt's August 2026 findings. Germany's authority concluded that the IDFA monopoly, combined with the asymmetric consent architecture, was sufficient to constitute a competition concern under Germany's special abuse provision for large digital companies. The UK claim invites the CAT to reach an analogous conclusion under the Chapter II prohibition of the Competition Act 1998 and, where applicable, residual EU law.Where Is the Case Now, and Who Should Pay Attention?The claim was filed at the CAT on September 3, 2026. Like all collective proceedings at the tribunal, it must first be certified — a threshold hearing at which the CAT will determine whether the claim meets the legal standards to proceed as a class action. Apple will almost certainly contest certification; in the Kent v Apple consumer case, Apple filed multiple failed procedural challenges over years before the case reached trial in January 2025.No certification hearing date has yet been set for the ATT claim.For UK-based app developers who released iOS apps between 2021 and the present and saw advertising revenue decline after ATT's launch, the opt-out structure means they are currently included in the class without taking any action. Developers who wish to step out of the claim before any compensation mechanism is established would need to actively opt out if and when the CAT certifies the claim and sets an opt-out window.For Apple, the financial exposure if the claim is certified and succeeds at trial would be the third largest damages bill in the CAT's history — behind only the ongoing appeal of the Kent v Apple judgment. It would also test, for the first time at the UK damages-recovery level, whether a privacy framework that real competition authorities in France, Italy, and Germany have already found problematic can simultaneously be treated as a pro-consumer feature rather than an anticompetitive tool. The two characterizations are not necessarily mutually exclusive — but the question of which one governs Apple's legal exposure is now squarely before a UK court.(Exchange rate as of September 4, 2026; conversions are approximate.)Frequently Asked QuestionsAm I included in the ATT Collective Action claim if I am a UK app developer?If you are or were a UK-based app developer who published iOS apps in the period covered by the claim, you are likely automatically included as a class member under the opt-out structure of the CAT's collective proceedings regime. This means you do not need to take any action to be part of the claim — but it also means you would need to actively opt out if you choose not to participate. No opt-out window has been opened because the claim is in its earliest stage; the CAT must first certify it before any class mechanics take effect. Watch the ATT Collective Action website and Hausfeld's communications for certification and opt-out deadlines when they are announced.Why does it matter that Apple's own apps were exempt from the ATT prompt?Apple's advertising business — its App Store Search Ads and related products — does not use the device's IDFA (Identifier for Advertisers) and does not combine data across third-party companies, which is what ATT specifically governs. This is why Apple says its own apps are legitimately exempt. The claimants' counterargument, supported by Germany's Bundeskartellamt finding, is that the asymmetry still conferred a competitive advantage: Apple's own consent prompts used neutral language while third-party apps were required to use Apple-designed wording that included a warning hand symbol and the word "tracking" — elements Germany found were engineered to discourage user consent for rivals while Apple's own prompts remained comparatively neutral. In short, the exemption may have been legally defensible in theory but was implemented in a way that tilted outcomes in practice.What did Germany's competition ruling actually require Apple to change?Under binding commitments accepted by the Bundeskartellamt on August 13, 2026 (case B7-54/25), Apple must within four months redesign the ATT consent prompt shown by third-party apps to remove discouraging wording and symbols — specifically the warning hand symbol and the word "tracking" — and rebalance the order and tone of choices to be more neutral. App publishers also gain the right to add up to 4,000 characters of explanatory text about why personalized ads fund their business, replacing Apple's previous one-to-two-sentence limit. Developers will be able to combine the ATT consent request with their GDPR data-protection consent into a single prompt rather than two separate asks. The commitments apply in Germany and, per Apple, in almost all other EU countries as well. An independent trustee will monitor compliance for seven years.
